description: In high muddy water after some rains, a flotilla of eight Common Mergansers in a straight line stretching all the way across Enlow Fork floated downstream to this spot and began milling about. They then entered the little (6’ wide) clearer stream that Smokey Row Road follows into the valley, and diving and splashing together were snapping up minnows faster than I could count - within 3-4 meters of me! They went up the stream for ten minutes, returned for a few minutes, then went back up the little stream (clearer H2O and easy pickings) for 20 minutes. I then walked up the road following the stream quite a ways but could not find them again. I wonder now if they were all immature siblings or if adults in eclipse plumage where among them, but I’m unclear how to distinguish them at this time of year.

description:
With Valeri Ponzo; Day 1 of our 3-day Thanksgiving holiday trip to the eastern Panhandle.

Our itinerary for Day 1 was:

0832-0948 EST: Forest Capital Museum State Park (Taylor County) -- our 71st state park birded together.

1041-1332 CST: Three Rivers State Park (Jackson County) -- our 72nd state park birded together.

1417-1710 CST: Chipola River Water Management Area (Calhoun County)

We spent the night at the Palmer Motel in Miday (only $44 with a $30 discount from booking.com!).

The weather at this site was cloudy and 64 degrees with a light breeze. We left at 1332 CST.

We barely saw the sun on any of the three days; most photographs were taken under gloomy skies, which meant that I often had to boost the light saturation to get a usable image, even if the image ended up looking washed-out.

Val and I have set goals of attaining 50 or more bird species in each of Florida's 67 counties (Val has reached or exceeded this total in 57 counties, while I have reached or exceeded 50 species in 56 counties; Val's hearing is much better than mine), along with visiting as many of the 175 (and ever-growing) tally of Florida state parks. From previous visits, I had already seen or heard 48 species in Jackson County (Val was already at 52 species), so we knew that we would get several species here -- as well as adding another state park to our list. This is a great spot; we hope to return some day.

He was alone and nearly passed out on the beach when we rolled up to camp, only moving to get into the shade of our cots. With no apparent means to feed himself, we thought he had only hours left. By the evening he was boldly snapping after dragonflies way too big for him. He started following us around any time one of us got up from a chair. Unfortunately, he vacated camp after he was unceremoniously shooed away for pooping on my brother’s shorts. I had been walking upriver to look at the plants, and was surprised to hear a coo. It was the baby bird! He was swimming, saw me, then tried to find the easiest path to shore to say hello. When I started walking back to camp, he followed me the whole 100 or so yards. Eventually, he wandered off into the twilight, presumably to start his own clan of rogue Rogue River mergansers. We named him Merlin.

description:
With Fran Meyerson; a surprisingly unsuccessful search for the Long-billed Curlew. We arrived in time for high tide, which saw all the shorebirds roosting together on the beach. I scanned every Marbled Godwit in the flock from the tower, 25-40 times each, always expecting to find the curlew when its head was not under its scapulars, but never finding it (I'm 98% positive that it was not present). The weather at the start was overcast, 65 degrees, and windy. At times, it was only mildly breezy, with maybe 7 minutes of sunlight. The entire flock took off at once at 1734 (final photo in the Western Willet record) and headed far south to roost elsewhere (there's no way that shorebirds would roost on a beach connected to the mainland; nocturnal mammalian predators would have a feast). We left at 1747, minutes after 7 American White Pelicans flee by offshore.

Below is our complete checklist:

3 Red-breasted Mergansers
1 Black-bellied Plover
97 Marbled Godwits
6 Ruddy Turnstones
6 Least Sandpipers
65 Short-billed Dowitchers
515 Willets
1 Ring-billed Gull
1 Forster's Tern
1 Royal Tern
1 Great Egret
1 Little Blue Heron
2 Red-bellied Woodpeckers
1 Nelson's Sparrow/Saltmarsh Sparrow
7 Palm Warblers

description:
Red-breasted Merganser (Mergus serrator) is a long-bodied waterfowl in the Ducks, Geese, and Swans (Anatidae) family. The red breast that gives the species its common name is only displayed by males in breeding plumage. It is a long-bodied duck with a long, pale orange bill and shaggy crest. Breeding males have a dark green head, brown breast, and gray sides. Females and immature males have a brown head and gray body. Bill is dull reddish-orange. It is distinguished from Common Merganser by a thinner bill, shaggier crest, and slimmer overall shape. It dives to catch fish on large bodies of water, including freshwater lakes, lagoons, and coastal regions. It favors saltwater more than the Common Merganser. Diet is mostly small fish, supplemented by crustaceans, aquatic insects, and sometimes frogs, tadpoles, or worms. Young ducklings mostly eat insects along the shoreline.

description:
With Don Fraser; my first visit here ... this year (?)! We skipped a walk-around survey and immediately settled into a Gulfwatch from the southern gazebo. The weather at the start was overcast, light sprinkling (which ended quickly), 64 degrees ("feels like" 64), with a light breeze. Once we found the Red-throated Loon, the survey sort of ended, as we were watching the loon while friends were en route to see it. Christine Rowland and Vince Capp arrived in time to see the loon, but Dave Bowman arrived a few minutes too late; the loon got up and flew north -- toward Hudson Marina -- after maybe 35 minutes. 

The Red-throated Loon was a NEW photographed bird for me for Florida!  And, it is the first photographically documented record for Pasco County! (Hudson Beach comes through again!).

The Helmeted Guineafowl was QUITE the surprise: according to Vince, it is imprinted on the Mallards and even follows them into the water!

Speaking of Mallards, we saw at least 42, with many aberrant plumages that I guess are the result of inbreeding.

We left at 0938 and headed to SunWest Park.

description:
Aripeka-Bayport Christmas Bird Count with Dave Bowman, Don Fraser, Dave Goodwin, Cecile Yarrow, Alice Herden,and others; a boat trip offered by Freedom Boat Club, with the boat -- a 10-person pontoon boat -- expertly captained by Sara Tunder. In its 32-year history, the Aripeka-Bayport CBC has never had an organized boat party. This year, Sara Tunder, the Community Investment Coordinator of the Freedom Boat Club, offered a boat trip for CBC participants. Three days later, a tour boat captain operating out of the same marina, photographed an American Flamingo -- the first record for Hernando County -- in the Hernando Beach Boat Channel! So, the timing to have a boat party for the CBC could not have been more timely or fortuitous. My party of the CBC, composed of three separate sub-parties this year, all participated on the boat trip; we also invited Charlie Fisher of another party, but he declined, wanting to cover his area more thoroughly.

I divided the observations from the boat trip into those seen from the boat while it was navigating the boat channel within Hernando Beach (onshore), and those from the boat while it was navigating the boat channel in the Gulf of Mexico (offshore).

We navigated as far as the westernmost spoil island, even though the last few spoil islands are out of the Aripeka-Bayport CBC circle. Some birds (for instance American Oystercatcher and Belted Kingfisher) photographed on the islands heading out may have been photographed again heading back, but as they would have been 30-90 minutes apart, then I am considering them to be independent and am listing them twice.

The weather at the start was overcast and 68 degrees ("feels like" 66) with a light breeze. We returned at 1415. The others called it a day while I drove to SunWest Park and continued birding on the CBC.

An absolutely epic trip!

description:
Hopefully the animated gif works! ***Update - you need to click on it to enlarge it, and then the first photo will show him diving.

In retrospect I had seen one or two of this species passing through occasionally in January, but they started hanging around virtually every day in February where I usually walk, and much like the heron from last fall, they became my new species to get obsessed with! If they’ve visited this particular stretch of the river in the last few years, it was not in these numbers and with this regularity, because this is part of my “commute” home from work, and I certainly would have noticed!

These grainy blurry pics are the best I could do with my phone, and I could barely see him with my actual eyes at times, so it was a tough ID at first since this species was new to me.

Impressions include: immediate “that’s not a mallard” bells ringing from a distance even though they’re about the same size and roughly similar-ish colors as a male, sits very low in the water even when not diving, *FAST* even when not diving (I have since seen individuals and small groups flying past, and they’re also super fast then, with what seems like short pointy wings with very white undersides), long skinny pointy little upturned pinkish beak, and then of course the diving, which “regular” ducks and geese  don’t do (I’m used to dabbling). They stay under for what seems like a really long time, 30-90 seconds usually, and pop up sometimes a good long distance away. Super fascinating, and I watched him for a long time trying to get better photos - there’s a ton of garbage on my album where he abruptly disappeared before I could get him, or where I failed to predict when/where he would surface again. I did eventually get a real camera and some good photos, but I want to keep a record of where I started.

***If it doesn’t auto-play for you, first image is an animated gif of 2 males doing a courtship display to 1 female. It’s called a “salute-curtsy’ which is very descriptive! “M’lady…”

This is what made me decide to get an actual camera, they were doing all sorts of cool behaviors and I could barely see them with my phone (or my nearsighted astigmatic eyeballs). .

Watched these guys for a long time, though looking at timestamps on the photos, not as long as it seemed because they cover a lot of distance very quickly. Pics posted in reverse order, I started on the west side and around the level of Roscoe, all 3 were intermittently diving and I didn’t get any photos at all, then for a stretch they were flapping and ducking/bathing and preening, terrible quality pics, then by the time we all got to Belmont, the boys started displaying. The guy on the right in most of these pics stayed much closer to the female and dipped more often, and tried to keep himself between her and the other guy most of the time, and occasionally swam right at him flicking his head a little, though no overt aggression/fights. The other guy would sometimes seem to start to leave but then always circled back again to rejoin them. For the next couple weeks I frequently saw 3 birds together, and I’m not sure if it was this same little trio repeatedly, or if that’s a common dynamic early in the season? By the end of February, I was mostly seeing either pairs or little mixed flocks of 5-8 birds with multiple males and multiple females.

description:
As great blue herons were to 2023, so red-breasted mergansers are to 2024: can’t stop taking pictures of them!

I saw this little group from both sides of the river and from the bridge. First few photos are from the east side after crossing, then a section to illustrate how great the zoom is on this new little camera compared to my phone - when I was on the bridge, they were rapidly heading north and already even with the dock as seen in the map screenshot. At this time I had not had any chance to watch tutorials on photography or camera settings (these pics are just things I see on my morning walk home after night shift!) so this was all just default/auto-focus - I have since started experimenting with faster shutter speeds and different settings, but I like how with these settings the water looks like a painting. Then the last two are when I first saw them from the west side - but by the time I zoomed in a bit more, they were all underwater!

Multiple shots in this series catching them diving, which is so cool to see in person. There might occasionally be a big fish that breaks the surface around here, but at this point if I see a group of concentric ripples like that in the middle of the river, I can pretty much guarantee there are mergansers in action - it’s just a question of how far away they will be when they surface. Unlike a jumping fish or a turtle splashing back into the water after basking, they’re also nearly silent when they dive and resurface. And from the wakes you can tell they go very fast, with seemingly very little effort.

description:
This is probably the same little group I saw diving about 20 minutes prior, but by the time I got to the boathouse dock, instead of diving they were doing courtship displays. I really wanted to catch some higher resolution shots of the “salute-curtsy” behavior as seen in terrible quality (but animated)  here: https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/201765824 but I was fighting with the auto-focus and they move very fast, so I had limited success, though you can see a few hints. description:
A pair of Merganser swimming in Lily Lake in the Northern Sierra.

Common Merganser (Mergus merganser) is a large duck with a sleek body and thin red bill. Breeding males have a dark green head and mostly white body with peachy blush on underparts. Females and immature males have a rusty brown head and gray bodies with a cleanly demarcated white throat. It feeds in rivers, lakes, and large ponds by diving to catch fish. It is hardy in winter, often staying as far north as open water permits before freezing.

Xeno-canto Bird songs, sound recordings, and species range map: https://xeno-canto.org/species/Mergus-merganser

"Conservation status: May be increasing in Europe; apparently stable in North America. Habitat is wooded lakes, rivers; in winter, rarely coastal bays. Mainly around fresh water at all seasons. Summer: on shallow but clear rivers and lakes in forested country; avoids dense marshes and muddy waters. Winter: on lakes, large rivers; occasionally on bays along coast.
This fish-eating duck is the typical merganser of freshwater lakes. Its flocks are usually small, but these may combine into big concentrations sometimes at large reservoirs. Common Mergansers living along rivers may spend hours resting on rocks or on shore. The British call this bird the 'Goosander.' In some parts of Europe, with artificial nesting sites provided, the species has become a common nesting bird along city waterfronts; this has not yet happened in North America."

description:
Female Red-breasted Merganser swimming in lagoon at mouth of Carmel River.

Red-breasted Merganser (Mergus serrator) is a long-bodied waterfowl in the Ducks, Geese, and Swans (Anatidae) family. The red breast that gives the species its common name is only displayed by males in breeding plumage. It is a long-bodied duck with a long, pale orange bill and shaggy crest. Breeding males have a dark green head, brown breast, and gray sides. Females and immature males have a brown head and gray body. Bill is dull reddish-orange. It is distinguished from Common Merganser by a thinner bill, shaggier crest, and slimmer overall shape. It dives to catch fish on large bodies of water, including freshwater lakes, lagoons, and coastal regions. It favors saltwater more than the Common Merganser. Diet is mostly small fish, supplemented by crustaceans, aquatic insects, and sometimes frogs, tadpoles, or worms. Young ducklings mostly eat insects along the shoreline.

description:
With Don Fraser; an eventually successful chase of the Purple Sandpiper. A few other birders were also looking for the sandpiper; at least one left before it was found. The weather at the start was clear and chilly with fairly strong north winds and a low tide, becoming sunny, warm, and breezy with a fairly high, still-incoming tide by the end. We walked from one jetty to the other numerous times, and to the boat ramp at the northern end of the peninsula twice. Eventually, Don stationed himself at the southern jetty while I stayed at the northern jetty, which proved to be the jetty popular with the birds. I stared at the same 22 Ruddy Turnstones dozens of times until 1229, when a flock of 33 turnstones arrived -- shorebirds and larids had been filtering in to the rocks on the north jetty for more than 90 minutes as the rising tide inundated all offshore oyster bars. Although none of us saw the Purple Sandpiper fly in, it must have arrived with the large turnstone flock, as Anne Ruben found it a minute later. I was between the Purple Sandpiper and the rest of the birds, so I waited until the sandpiper flew to join all the other birds before I moved. All in all, it was a fun trip -- except for the ubiquitous kids and others who habitually harassed the Black Skimmers and other birds that were trying to rest on the beach.

description: Females. Photo#5 with male. Photo#6 with smaller female Hooded Merganser
A lot of babies with her!
I think this is an immature male common merganser.

Large mergansers with richer colors and higher contrasts than RBME and a clean demarcation between head and neck, a cleanly defined white area at the chin. It took a while to review these birds as they appeared different from each other and they appear to be 2021 (SY) birds. Diving in, it turns out they are the most difficult of our three mergansers to age, and to sex when they are young. They both had yellow, not brown eyes (e.g. eye color of more mature birds)
https://macaulaylibrary.org/asset/305929581
https://macaulaylibrary.org/asset/377271211

The one in the bay had more consistently grey sides (and when it flew a narrow black line showed at the tips of all the greater coverts, including the inner ones), whereas the one in QMR had a lot of white marbling in the grey on its sides, just in front of the bend of the wing (perhaps a male? in study), and it also had a more richly colored bill. It had two grey feathers sitting over the white speculum on either wing, and a couple of dark grey feathers coming in midway on the sides at the water line. Both had a dark stripe on the culmen. Just to double check I went back and found the one on the bay, snoozing with RBMG (37.806848, -122.457217) then rode over to QMR and three minutes later the marbled one was foraging in the creek that leads south.

More research netted an article called "Mergansers: ID, ageing and sexing" by Tony Leukering. He writes, "... >500 photos of Common Mergansers in the eBird/Macaulay Library photo archive2 (Sullivan 2009) and at Flickr3 and found <8 photos of Common Mergansers that I could determine (via plumage, eye color) were immature males, even when restricting my search to November through May. Conversely, there are numerous photos of immature male Red-breasted Mergansers discoverable with similar searches. I suspect that many or most immature male Common Mergansers make the transition to adult-like plumage quite late, if at all. One of the causes of this relative lack of photographic material of immature male Commons in plumage transition may be due to its relatively earlier spring migration (personal observation, eBird 20124), which could mean that the molt takes place mostly on or near the breeding grounds, where they are less accessible to most photographers. ... adult males attain a variably female-like plumage May-July and molt out of that plumage August-October (Pyle 2008, Dugger et al. 2009, Craik et al. 2015, Pearce et al. 2015)"

So these aren't adult males in alternate (dull) plumage (it's flipped around in ducks, haha ... a few months ago you'd likely need to see an open wing to sex adults) as we've seen those fly by recently in bright plumage, so, timing.

M.m. americanus by the feathering at the base of the upper mandible looks like a "2" (on the nominate and orientalis it looks like a 'Z'), the nostrils are found midway on the bill, and lack of a hook at the tip. Compare the eurostyle:
https://macaulaylibrary.org/asset/404746081
